25 A train’s whistle is emitting sound of frequency 500 Hz as the train moves with a speed of 20 m s–1
along a straight track. The train moves directly towards a stationary observer standing next to the
track and then passes the observer.
The speed of sound in air is 330 m s–1.
What is the difference between the frequencies of the sound heard by the observer before and
after the train has passed the observer?
A
29 Hz
B
32 Hz
C
40 Hz
D
61 Hz
© UCLES 2021

hints: Notice the observer hears a higher $500 \text{Hz}$ whistle while the $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ train approaches and a lower pitch after it passes, so you need two observed frequencies.
Connect this to the Doppler effect for a moving source: use $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$ when approaching and $f_o = f_s v/(v + v_s)$ when receding, with $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Calculate both frequencies in $\text{Hz}$ and then subtract the receding value from the approaching value to get the before-minus-after difference.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: source frequency $f_s = 500 \text{Hz}$, source speed $v_s = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, wave speed $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, with a stationary observer.
Recall the moving-source Doppler rule: waves are crowded ahead of the train and stretched behind it, so divide by $v - v_s$ before passing and by $v + v_s$ after passing.
Find the difference heard before and after passing: $f_{approach} - f_{recede} \approx 532.3 - 471.4 \approx 60.9 \text{Hz}$, about $61 \text{Hz}$ with correct units. This is option D.

A.explanation: About $29 \text{Hz}$ is close to only half the total shift, from $500 \text{Hz}$ to the receding frequency alone.

B.explanation: About $32 \text{Hz}$ is close to only half the total shift, from $500 \text{Hz}$ to the approaching frequency alone.

C.explanation: About $40 \text{Hz}$ underestimates the change because it does not use $v/(v \pm v_s)$ with $v=330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v_s=20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ correctly.

D.explanation: The approaching frequency near $532 \text{Hz}$ minus the receding frequency near $471 \text{Hz}$ gives about $61 \text{Hz}$.
